title: Sensor Placement, Mapping, and Calibration
objective: Build a traceable environmental measurement system that distinguishes representative control sensors, diagnostic mapping instruments, and independent safety devices.

terms.definition: Comparison with a traceable reference and adjustment or documented correction when permitted.
Check that an instrument performs within a defined tolerance without necessarily adjusting it.
Sensor whose signal drives equipment or automation.
Quantified doubt associated with a measurement result.

coreScience: A sensor measures its own location and exposure. Direct fixture radiation, cold walls, supply jets, humidifier plumes, wet leaves, irrigation splash, body heat, and poor shielding can bias temperature, RH, CO2, and leaf-temperature readings. Representative placement is a design decision, not whatever wall position is convenient.

Control and mapping require different architectures. A stable shielded canopy-level control sensor may drive HVAC, while a grid of portable or fixed sensors reveals spatial distribution. Independent safety sensors should not be treated as interchangeable with plant-control sensors, especially for CO2.

Calibration is more than pressing a reset button. It requires an appropriate reference, stabilization time, defined points across the operating range, as-found and as-left results, tolerance, adjustment authority, and traceability. RH sensors can drift or become contaminated; substrate probes require medium-specific validation; CO2 sensors may show age, cross-sensitivity, or placement bias.

Radiative and airflow bias. Unshielded temperature probes can absorb fixture radiation; supply jets, humidifier plumes and cold boundaries create local microclimates. A sensor's exposure and response time determine whether its reading represents nearby leaves.

Spatial sampling. A canopy map records position, height and operating state. Repeat readings across lights-on, lights-off and transitions; a single mean can conceal important hotspots and humidity gradients.

Calibration and verification. Verification compares an instrument against an appropriate reference and acceptance criterion. Calibration establishes a measurement relationship and uncertainty; adjustment is a separate action. Preserve as-found results, reference identity and as-left results when adjusted.

Independent safety measurements. A horticultural CO₂ control sensor cannot substitute for a properly specified, located and maintained occupational safety alarm. Failure modes, setpoints and purpose differ.
cultivationRelevance: Create a sensor register with unique IDs, model, serial number, range, accuracy specification, location, height, shield, calibration history, battery or power status, and data-system channel. Flag substituted or moved sensors as controlled changes.

Map the occupied canopy under representative peak and transition conditions. Synchronize clocks, compare overlapping instruments, quarantine implausible data, and retain raw values when corrections are applied.
Document sensor IDs, exact heights and locations, shielding, model specifications, data channels and calibration records before interpreting trends.
Perform side-by-side comparisons after stabilization, investigate disagreements and map multiple canopy zones under representative operating conditions.
Keep original data, clock synchronization and change history when moving probes or applying corrections. Confirm changes with a repeat map.

Clock sync, gaps, spikes, drift, correction factor, quarantine, and replacement.
Operating state, grid, statistics, zones, corrective action, and remap approval.

misconceptions: A new sensor is calibrated for this room: Factory specification does not prove field placement or current agreement with a reference.
Two sensors that disagree can be averaged: The cause must be investigated before combining biased data.
More sensors automatically improve control: Poor placement, drift, and unsynchronized data can multiply confusion.
evidenceLimits: Calibration methods and tolerances depend on sensor technology and intended use. Follow manufacturer instructions, safety standards, and traceability requirements for the actual instrument.
The diagram is an illustrative placement comparison, not a measured temperature or humidity map.
Appropriate tolerances and calibration procedures are technology- and use-specific; manufacturer instructions and relevant standards govern.
Co-located agreement does not establish spatial representativeness or absolute accuracy unless reference uncertainty and exposure are controlled.

overview: Environmental sensors report conditions at the probe, not automatically the crop's entire microclimate. Reliable control requires deliberate placement, representative spatial mapping, traceable checks and separation of control sensors from independent safety devices.
